slides.title: What Is Method Overloading
slides.content: Method overloading lets you define multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists within the same class.
slides.example:
void Print(int x) { }
void Print(string s) { }
slides.exampleOutput: Declaration or expression only; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: What is the same in overloaded methods?

slides.title: Parameter Differences
slides.content: Overloaded methods must differ by parameter count, type, or order. The return type alone is not enough to overload.
slides.example:
int Get() => 0;
string Get() => "A"; // compile error
slides.exampleOutput: Declaration or expression only; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: To overload by return type alone is _____.

slides.title: Compile-Time Polymorphism
slides.content: The compiler selects the correct overload at compile time based on the arguments passed. This is also called static polymorphism.
slides.exampleOutput: Declaration or expression only; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: Drag the term for overload resolution at compile time: [?] polymorphism

slides.title: Common Overload Patterns
slides.content: A common pattern provides a full method and a simplified one with fewer parameters, often using optional or params.
slides.example:
void Log(string msg, int level) { }
void Log(string msg) => Log(msg, 0);
slides.exampleOutput: Declaration or expression only; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: Complete the overload so calling Add(5) returns 5 + 1 = 6.
exercise.starterCode:
int Add(int x, int y) => x + y;
int Add(int x) => Add(x, _____);
hints: Make sure your code includes the required keywords/elements: x + 1, x, 1
When run, your code should output: 6

slides.title: Optional Parameters vs Overloading
slides.content: Optional parameters provide default values. Overloading is clearer when defaults depend on complex logic.
slides.example:
void Connect(string url, int port = 80) { }
void Connect(string url) => Connect(url, 443);
slides.exampleOutput: Declaration or expression only; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: Which approach is better when default behavior is complex?

slides.title: Params Keyword
slides.content: The params keyword allows a variable number of arguments. It is not overloading by itself but can complement it.
slides.exampleOutput: No console output is produced by this code in this example.

exercise.prompt: Complete the parameter declaration: void Sum(_____ int[] numbers)

slides.title: Ambiguous Overloads
slides.content: If two overloads could match, the compiler may report ambiguity. Exact matches are preferred over conversions.
slides.exampleOutput: Declaration or expression only; produces no console output.

slides.title: Method Overloading Review
slides.content: Overloading improves readability by using one method name for related operations. Keep overloads intuitive and consistent.

exercise.prompt: Write two overloads named Display: one takes a string, one takes an int. Each prints its value.
hints: Make sure your code includes the required keywords/elements: Console.WriteLine
When run, your code should output: Compiles and prints correctly.
